title: Scaling laws
description: Held-out loss follows regular trends with model size, data, and compute.

claims.heading: Held-out language-model loss follows power laws when other resources are sufficient
Power laws fitted on small runs predict loss at much larger scales
Optimal model size and training tokens scale as powers of compute within training setups
Depth and width change loss little across moderate shapes at fixed parameter count
Power laws extend beyond text pretraining under specific conditions
Downstream performance improves predictably with scale or lower pretraining loss
Scaling exponents and optimal compute allocation depend on setup and fitting choices

related_findings.title: Improvements across modalities do not establish shared laws
related_findings.summary: Larger models, more data, or longer training often improve measured performance across modalities. Unfitted sweeps and confounded comparisons leave shared functional forms and reliable extrapolation unestablished.

examples.headline: Larger parallel-only translation models improve BLEU without establishing a fitted law or forecast.
More sleep2vec pretraining data improves Macro-F1, without consistently diminishing gains or a fitted scaling function.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Architecture can improve efficiency while preserving scaling slopes
related_findings.summary: Architecture and training changes can improve loss or resource efficiency while leaving fitted scaling exponents approximately unchanged.

examples.headline: Local SGD and distributed data parallelism have similar parameter-scaling exponents with equal batch sizes and data.
Block AttnRes matches a baseline using more compute while preserving nearly identical fitted slopes.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Data quality changes resource efficiency
related_findings.summary: Data relevance and selection can improve performance per token or unit of compute. Benefits depend on the task, scale, evaluation, and selection cost.

examples.headline: Learnability-based selection saves about 25–33% compute at matched accuracy, including selection cost.
With matched 500M architectures, DCLM's data mixture beats RefinedWeb+StarCoder's mixture in average accuracy using fewer tokens.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Optimization changes scaling and preferred hyperparameters
related_findings.summary: Preferred learning rates, batches, and schedules depend on the scaling setting. Optimization choices also change stability, efficiency, loss floors, and apparent exponents.

examples.headline: Critical batch-size exponents differ when model and data grow together versus when data stays fixed.
Joint learning-rate and weight-decay tuning sharply reduces Muon-SW's advantage over constant decay.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Preferred model shapes depend on the task
related_findings.summary: Depth, width, and component allocation can change downstream quality at similar model size or compute. Preferred shapes depend on the task, data, and training objective.

examples.headline: At equal size, wider models improve GPT-2 GLUE scores but reduce RoBERTa scores.
After 1M training videos, wide-shallow AR-k=1 outperforms the similarly sized deep-narrow model.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Lower loss does not guarantee better task performance
related_findings.summary: Loss can track downstream performance within controlled settings. Changes in architecture, data mixture, adaptation, or evaluation can break that relationship.

examples.headline: Reweighted supervised fine-tuning lowers Llama3.1-70B perplexity on Orca while reducing its average downstream score.
At matched compute, mixture-of-experts has best test loss but lowest average score on Core 9 benchmark.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Individual metrics can worsen as scale increases
related_findings.summary: Particular tasks and metrics can plateau or worsen as parameters, data, or training increase, even when aggregate performance improves.

examples.headline: Doubling PPG-MAE encoder depth leaves heart-rate error unchanged and worsens heart-rate-variability errors.
Across reported ranges, CreditRisk's Kolmogorov–Smirnov score on later data falls with more unlabeled data or parameters.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Transfer depends on alignment and training choices
related_findings.summary: Pretraining benefits, adaptation efficiency, and forgetting depend on source–target alignment, capacity, data, and updated components. Transfer can weaken or reverse as these conditions change.

examples.headline: Model size and training steps predict forgetting better than fine-tuning loss alone.
Mixing scarce domain data into pretraining lowers post-finetuning domain loss and required tokens.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Data and target structure shape scaling regimes
related_findings.summary: Solvable and toy models connect exponents, floors, and transitions to data spectra, target structure, noise, and capacity. Curve shape alone need not identify the underlying mechanism.

examples.headline: Zipf feature frequencies determine theoretical error exponents that closely match a memorizing classifier's fitted exponents.
Softmax teacher–student loss decays as a power law at low temperature, exponentially at high temperature.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Resource allocation depends on objectives and constraints
related_findings.summary: Preferred allocations of capacity, data, and training depend on the objective, modality, data limits, and lifecycle costs. They can differ from allocations that minimize pretraining loss.

examples.headline: Counting action-generation compute yields an intermediate optimal reinforcement-learning model size; learner-only accounting favors larger models.
A fitted downstream-error law favors more data; predicted optimal allocations were not tested by training models.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: More inference effort helps under suitable conditions
related_findings.summary: Sampling, ensembles, search, and interaction can improve quality or coverage with diminishing returns. Realized gains depend on diversity, selection, feedback, calibration, and the task.

examples.headline: Coverage with perfect answer selection keeps improving for Llama-3-8B-Instruct; majority voting and reward-model selection plateau.
Feedback-adjusted resources better predict synthetic-task failure; stronger feedback improves success at matched raw budgets.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Architecture can change scaling slopes
related_findings.summary: Architecture, parameterization, and inductive bias can change fitted exponents, crossovers, and useful scaling regimes.

examples.headline: At equal weight counts, group-equivariant CNNs show steeper data scaling than CNNs on rotation-invariant images.
On C4, LayerRoPE has a larger fitted compute exponent than Pre-Norm with a shared asymptote.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Repeated data has conditional and diminishing value
related_findings.summary: Repeated data can help before saturation or overfitting. Its effective value and the best stopping point depend on capacity, repetition, objective, and optimization.

examples.headline: Repeated epochs initially improve recommendation loss, then saturate, with overfitting in the larger model.
Repeated-token value falls across epochs and rises with tokens per parameter.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Useful data mixtures change with scale
related_findings.summary: Domain and modality proportions affect loss, transfer, and interference. Useful mixtures can change with model size, compute, training stage, and target domain.

examples.headline: Fitted domain-ratio laws accurately predict held-out mixture losses after continued pretraining.
At fixed size and tokens, ShapleyLaw predicts unseen language mixtures better than FamilyLaw.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Extrapolation depends on fitting choices
related_findings.summary: Forecasts and derived resource requirements depend on functional form, fitting range, training information, and uncertainty estimation. Good local fits need not yield stable predictions at larger scales.

examples.headline: Chinchilla bootstrap refits from scratch give much wider allocation-exponent uncertainty than refits initialized with fitted parameters.
A Chinchilla-form fit forecasts larger-scale losses less accurately than the cited Delphi-team forecast or residual TabPFN.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Representations have scaling patterns beyond mean loss
related_findings.summary: Representation geometry, rank, features, and information measures have their own dependence on scale and training. These measures can show thresholds and reversals absent from mean loss.

examples.headline: The reduction in representation curvature grows approximately logarithmically with GPT-2 model size.
Activation for category concepts, measured with sparse autoencoders, jumps between Pythia 160M and 410M, then plateaus.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Sparse capacity and active compute contribute separately
related_findings.summary: Sparse-model loss depends jointly on total capacity, active computation, routing, and expert allocation. Preferred sparsity changes with scale, data, and objective.

examples.headline: Increasing total capacity in sparse-depth models lowers loss with fixed compute and capacity used per pass.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Context and prompting gains depend on conditions
related_findings.summary: Context, demonstrations, and reasoning prompts provide additional scaling axes. Their gains, saturation, and reversals depend on the task, architecture, and training.

examples.headline: Llama 3 8B retrieval-augmented in-context learning accuracy saturates exponentially as demonstrations increase.
Two-shot prompting raises Llama 3.1 8B F1 but lowers Llama 3.3 70B F1.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Task-aligned proxies can predict downstream performance
related_findings.summary: Task-aligned losses, related benchmarks, and representation measures can predict later or adapted performance. Their validity depends on proxy construction, the task, and adaptation protocol.

examples.headline: HE-SNR on filtered Action tokens predicts post-SFT SWE-bench scores better than on Thinking tokens.
A capability score from text benchmarks predicts derived vision-language model accuracy, including with a 72B backbone.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Safety and robustness need separate scaling analyses
related_findings.summary: Safety, fairness, calibration, robustness, and answer stability have different scaling trends across metrics and model families. Prompting, attacks, corruption, and relative attacker capacity can alter those trends.

examples.headline: Black-to-white false-positive-rate disparities increase with model size and vary with the prompt condition.
Relative attacker-to-target model size correlates with judged harm in jailbreak exchanges.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Narrow observations leave scaling laws unestablished
related_findings.summary: Single training trajectories and narrow size comparisons can show falling or flattening loss without establishing power laws or quantitative prediction across scales.

examples.headline: Yuan 245B training loss falls rapidly early in training and then flattens.
At fixed training tokens, larger baseline models lower validation loss without establishing a functional form.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Fine-tuning data can show early saturation
related_findings.summary: Adaptation gains depend on data amount, difficulty, and task diversity. Returns can diminish, plateau, or reverse depending on the model and method.

examples.headline: InternVL gains more up to 30K fine-tuning samples than from the subsequent increase to 100K.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Shared parameters support additional computation
related_findings.summary: Recurrence, weight sharing, and parallel streams add computation without proportional growth in stored parameters. Benefits depend on how compute is counted, training duration, how model components are connected, and the range of iteration counts.

examples.headline: Looping blocks in a fixed 170M diffusion language model matches baseline loss with fewer training FLOPs.
More LoopFormer inference loops lower Pile perplexity and improve average zero-shot accuracy.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Precision penalties depend on size and training
related_findings.summary: Precision changes effective capacity and resource allocation. Quantization penalties depend separately on model size, training duration, granularity, and method.

examples.headline: Pythia loss penalties with the GPTQ quantization method depend jointly on size, training tokens, and precision.
At 30M parameters, longer training increases the INT6 penalty.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Average gains can conceal uneven outcomes
related_findings.summary: Aggregate improvements can coexist with individual regressions, subgroup disparities, rare-task plateaus, and weak transfer outside the training distribution.

examples.headline: Video diffusion improves in-distribution velocity prediction while out-of-distribution errors remain far above the parsing baseline.
Regional-English bits-per-byte gaps change unevenly; their rates of change correlate with online speaker population.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Small-run rankings transfer unevenly
related_findings.summary: Small or short runs can inform training choices, but ranking preservation depends on the proxy, task, noise, scale gap, and training stage.

examples.headline: Tokenizer rankings transfer strongly for translation, weakly for multiple choice, and poorly for X-SUM.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Inference allocation depends on task and cost
related_findings.summary: The useful split between model size, inputs, sampling, reasoning, retrieval, and verification depends on the task, budget, training, and hardware cost accounting.

examples.headline: Under fixed inference FLOPs, visual reasoning prefers bigger LLMs, fewer visual tokens; OCR reverses this.
Memory-aware accounting favors larger models before more long CoT or Best-of-N, up to model-dependent sizes.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Tasks and metrics determine scaling forms
related_findings.summary: Task performance, generation quality, and loss components can follow logarithmic, power-law, or exponential relations. Forms and exponents depend on difficulty, dimensionality, floors, and training regime.

examples.headline: AlphaZero playing-strength exponents differ across games, with Oware's estimate limited by insufficient training.
With quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA), factual inconsistency generally fits exponential size dependence better than power laws.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Training schedules help predict loss trajectories
related_findings.summary: Models that account for learning-rate schedules, and normalization methods, can help predict how loss changes during training across scales. Prediction reliability depends on past learning rates, training tokens per model parameter, and how long the optimizer’s effects persist.

examples.headline: Schedule-aware predictions outperform a simplified Chinchilla-style rule relating loss to scale across varied learning-rate schedules.
A normalized model predicts larger-model loss curves given schedules, tokens per parameter, and AdamW’s response timescale.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Larger models can need fewer training examples
related_findings.summary: Larger models or pretraining can reduce the examples or updates needed for target performance. Benefits depend on labels, data relevance, and optimization.

examples.headline: The large model needs fewer images than the tiny model for fine-tuning and 10-example/class transfer.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Input representation changes effective scale
related_findings.summary: Tokenization, vocabulary, image resolution, and the allocation of visual tokens change how much data a model effectively sees and how efficiently it uses resources. Preferred choices depend on the model, modality, data regime, and task.

examples.headline: Preferred vocabulary size decreases with scarce data and increases with excess data.
At equal compute, byte models trail BPE on the shorter budget, lead on the longer.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Model size alone does not determine rankings
related_findings.summary: Across differently trained families and releases, model size, training tokens, and release date do not determine downstream rankings or isolate scale effects.

examples.headline: Smaller Flan-T5-XL and mT0-XL outperform Llama-2 7B on PHOENIX14T translation, but family differences prevent isolating size.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Capacity, data, and training must grow together
related_findings.summary: Benefits from larger models or datasets depend jointly on capacity, unique data, and training duration. Scaling one resource while another remains limiting can saturate or worsen performance.

examples.headline: R50x1 can transfer worse after JFT-300M pretraining than after ImageNet-21k pretraining.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Reinforcement-learning scaling depends on architecture and difficulty
related_findings.summary: Reinforcement-learning curves depend on architecture, base capability, task difficulty, algorithm, and rollout or update allocation. Scaling can produce improvement, saturation, or reversal.

examples.headline: Simply widening Rainbow’s networks lowers performance scores; adding Soft MoE’s softly routed expert networks improves them.
Greater expressiveness makes Qwen3 reinforcement-learning training steps rise faster with proofs’ reasoning depth in power-law fits.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Metrics can create apparent scaling transitions
related_findings.summary: Data support, task compatibility, acquisition order, and thresholds can produce cliffs or plateaus. Discrete metrics can also show abrupt changes over smoothly improving loss.

examples.headline: Discrete retrieval metrics improve sharply despite smoothly scaling continuous loss.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Data coverage matters separately from volume
related_findings.summary: Source, domain, subject, and spatial or temporal coverage describe data resources beyond volume. Their benefits can saturate or disappear depending on information content and evaluation.

examples.headline: At matched unique sample volume, spreading data across more subjects gives no detectable downstream benefit.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Hardware costs change practical scaling optima
related_findings.summary: Latency, memory traffic, storage, power, and hardware utilization change which resource trade-offs are achievable in practice and which configurations are preferred, beyond what theoretical FLOP counts indicate.

examples.headline: Fits accounting for hardware favor intermediate mixture-of-experts sparsity; optimizing model floating-point operation counts favors an extreme.
On one consumer GPU with finite data, optimal model size grows with wall-clock training time.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Post-training changes capabilities without changing model size
related_findings.summary: Instruction tuning, preference optimization, and objective changes shift downstream abilities at fixed model size, with task-dependent gains and losses.

examples.headline: Instruction-tuned Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B score higher on CyberMetric than their base models.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Evaluation choices change apparent scaling
related_findings.summary: Prompts, formatting, answer extraction, judges, contamination, and evaluation distributions can change measured scaling curves and model rankings.

examples.headline: Accepting more answer formats resolves an apparent drop in Qwen 3B’s GSM8K score.
Fixing substring-matching errors substantially raises Llama 3.3 70B’s F1, a score combining precision and recall.

related_findings.title: Memory adds capacity beyond the main network
related_findings.summary: Auxiliary memory, recurrent state, virtual width (effective network width), and the capacity to represent information can change loss or recall beyond what the main network’s size provides. Gains in loss or recall depend on architecture and remaining bottlenecks.

examples.headline: Larger auxiliary memory lowers validation BPB for Bigram and MoME at fixed backbone and compute.

related_findings.title: Factual recall depends on capacity and exposure
related_findings.summary: More parameters can increase memorization and the capacity to store factual associations. Recall also depends on exposure, repetition, architecture, and training choices.

examples.headline: Fact-storage capacity scales linearly with parameters outside embedding layers in the tested company-table and Wikidata settings.
Binding capacity follows a size relation in frozen small LMs, while broader model comparisons vary unevenly.

related_findings.title: Human alignment depends on the measure
related_findings.summary: Alignment with human reading, judgments, and brain responses depends on language, corpus, layer, and training stage. Some measures improve with scale while others plateau or reverse.

examples.headline: Perplexity tracks prediction quality for English eye-fixation durations; its relation reverses direction across Japanese perplexity ranges.
Some best-layer brain-alignment differences across model sizes are not significant; results vary by family.

related_findings.title: Optimization and reuse can change theoretical exponents
related_findings.summary: In solvable models, optimization, training schedules, data reuse, and depth can change how fast performance changes with training time and how resources are allocated. Benefits depend on how much each pattern that can be learned separately contributes to learning, task conditions, training stability, and the range of values used to fit the scaling law.

examples.headline: Simulated multi-pass sketched linear regression shows steeper data scaling than one-pass stochastic gradient descent.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Component compatibility governs pipeline gains
related_findings.summary: The benefits of distillation and evaluation depend on how well the components work together, what the student model can represent, and how resources are allocated. Larger teachers, models that assign rewards, or models that check answers need not improve downstream outcomes.

examples.headline: Larger students generally gain more from distillation; average student performance often falls with larger teachers.

related_findings.title: Model reuse and growth can save training resources
related_findings.summary: Growing or reusing pretrained models can reduce resources needed for target performance. Savings depend on the growth method, checkpoint history, and training stage.

examples.headline: Growing Dialog-GPT checkpoints reaches scratch-trained loss sooner, with smaller savings for larger enlargements.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Recommendation scaling depends on architecture and data handling
related_findings.summary: Recommendation quality depends jointly on architecture, depth, cached history, features, and data breadth. Increasing one resource can saturate or degrade performance.

examples.headline: Recommendation gains from depth depend on architecture; GPT and SASRec performance drops sharply beyond certain depths.
DCN-V2 LogLoss remains nearly flat with size, while Zenith++ improves across model tiers.

related_findings.title: Pruning tolerance depends on task and method
related_findings.summary: Pruning and compression effects depend on severity, model, method, task, and recovery training. Similar response shapes need not imply uniform losses across abilities.

examples.headline: Maximum sparsity within a 5% relative accuracy drop varies across tasks, pruning methods and models.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Theoretical allocation depends on modeling assumptions
related_findings.summary: Solvable models and statistical bounds imply how resources should be divided. How that division scales depends on how much each pattern that can be learned separately contributes to learning, how smoothly the relevant functions change with their inputs, the task’s structure, and limits on what the model can represent.

examples.headline: Optimizing a theoretical bound on avoidable error favors more data over more parameters used per prediction.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Retrieval adds another scaling resource
related_findings.summary: Retrieval capacity, datastore size, and resources used at inference can improve performance. Gains depend on the capacity of the model that reads retrieved information, what it encounters and how often during training, the data distribution, and the evaluation metric.

examples.headline: At equal compute, RA-CM3 improves perplexity over vanilla CM3 across the tested model sizes.
Larger inference-time datastores lower perplexity for tested Llama models without reported saturation through 1.4T tokens.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Synthetic data can reduce errors or introduce plateaus
related_findings.summary: Adding synthetic data can reduce error while introducing a lower limit set by systematic bias. Repeated cycles of generating data to train the next model, incompatible training targets, and mismatches in the learning setup can change rates of learning or cause performance to deteriorate.

examples.headline: GPT-4 Turbo augmentation reduces classifier errors, but Gender error rises beyond the reported best synthetic ratio.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Scale changes output diversity and error composition
related_findings.summary: Scaling can change diversity, copying, hallucination, and reasoning-error structure alongside aggregate accuracy.

examples.headline: Chemical-generation novelty eventually declines exponentially as the number of generations grows.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Algorithmic progress reduces compute requirements
related_findings.summary: Historical analyses attribute part of model progress to algorithmic changes that reduce compute requirements. Estimates depend on how progress and compute are measured.

examples.headline: Estimated compute for fixed language-model perplexity halves every 8.4 months, with substantial uncertainty.

related_findings.title: Human judgments can improve with scale
related_findings.summary: Human judgments of generated text and speech can improve with model or joint model–data scale. Returns diminish over some tested ranges.

examples.headline: BASE-medium improves naturalness over BASE-small; BASE-large adds a significant gain only for Male speaker A.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Checkpoint averaging changes returns to training compute
related_findings.summary: Splitting training compute across independent runs and averaging their checkpoints can improve the performance achievable for a given compute budget compared with extending a single run.

examples.headline: At fixed mixture-of-experts size, combining selected saved model versions improves performance after single-run mid-training progress plateaus.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Scaling gains can reach productivity and revenue
related_findings.summary: Reported scaling-related gains extend to worker productivity and advertising revenue. Benefits depend on worker skill, configuration, and how offline quality translates into deployment outcomes.

examples.headline: Higher training compute for translation-assistance models correlates with workers’ faster translations and higher earnings per minute.
Feature-expanded advertising MLPs produce revenue gains close to the reported predictions.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Benefits of simulation accuracy depend on the prediction target
related_findings.summary: Mixing simulations with different levels of detail or accuracy can use a fixed budget more efficiently. Which mixtures help, and whether results extrapolate, depend on the quantity being predicted, the gap between simulation accuracy levels, and sudden shifts in which choice is optimal.

examples.headline: Multi-fidelity PDE-surrogate training saves data-generation budget at matched relative L2 error.
Wall-shear-stress prediction shows no positive low-fidelity transfer and larger fidelity gaps than pressure.

related_findings.title: Scaling can improve decoding efficiency under some conditions
related_findings.summary: The number of proposed tokens accepted per decoding step and the amount of parallel processing can increase with training or scale. Data efficiency and the point at which gains level off depend on architecture.

examples.headline: A fit predicts tokens/call for a 3B model excluded from fitting; root-mean-square prediction error: 0.010.

reading_list.why: Introduces language-model loss laws and compute allocation estimates that later studies test and revise.
Revises compute allocation toward balanced growth in model size and training data, with estimates varying across fitting methods.
Uses new training runs and ablations to show how compute accounting and training choices change optimal model-size scaling.

known_gaps.summary: The main gaps concern extrapolation range, controlled scaling and allocation tests, comparable conditions, domain dependence, fitting uncertainty, and independent evidence.
items: Several forecasting studies test only limited distances beyond their fitting range. Their validation designs and quantitative reporting do not establish accuracy across multiple orders of magnitude.

For DriveGPT and weather models, the optimal split between model size and training data remains uncertain and, in some cases, unidentified: studies lack allocation exponents or full curves showing the lowest achievable loss at each compute budget. Observational fits against compute also lack controlled tests that vary this split.

ESN/BabyLM saturation and worsening validation loss were observed under a fixed one-epoch budget without a fitted power law. Whether these trends persist without resource bottlenecks remains unresolved.
It remains unclear whether the reported scaling results for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models conflict when tested under sufficiently similar conditions.

The relationship between Paloma's loss measurements and task performance depends on the evaluation domain and pretraining data. Comparisons at a fixed model size do not establish forecasts across model scales.

Some fitting-method comparisons lack uncertainty estimates and show only small effects. Changes in the exponents describing loss need to be distinguished from changes in those describing the optimal allocation between model size and training data.

It is not yet established whether recurring findings about how compute is allocated during inference and what numerical precision is used come from independent evidence. Author overlap, reused experiments and differences in tested conditions need examination.
